input: In this worked example, we consider a continuous stirred-tank reactor in which a neutralisation reaction is carried out, with the reaction being first order in the limiting reactant. At the operating temperature of the reactor, the rate constant is 0.241 min-1, and the mean residence time of the material in the vessel is 28 min. By applying the well-known steady-state design equation for an ideal CSTR, the conversion of the limiting reactant can be estimated at 87.1%. It is important to note that this estimate rests on a number of underlying assumptions, most notably the assumption of perfect mixing throughout the vessel and the assumption of constant density. In practice, it should also be borne in mind that tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run, which means that the true residence time distribution may well deviate from the ideal behaviour that has been assumed here. As a result, the conversion of 87.1% should be regarded as an idealised estimate rather than a guaranteed operating value. This type of calculation is widely used as a first estimate in reactor design, as it provides a rapid indication of the level of performance that can be expected before more detailed modelling is undertaken. Nevertheless, the simplicity of the approach should not be allowed to obscure the fact that real vessels rarely behave in a perfectly ideal fashion, and dead zones, bypassing, and other departures from ideal mixing can all have an impact on the conversion that is actually achieved in practice.
target: A continuous stirred-tank reactor runs a neutralisation that is first order in the limiting reactant. The rate constant is 0.241 min-1 at the operating temperature, and the mean residence time is 28 min. The worked example asks for the steady-state conversion of the limiting reactant in an ideal CSTR. For a first-order reaction in a perfectly mixed vessel, conversion is fixed by the rate constant and the residence time together: a longer residence time or a faster reaction converts more, and the two quantities enter as a product. On the stated values, the conversion is 87.1%. The estimate assumes perfect mixing and constant density. Perfect mixing is the assumption that carries the number. It makes the concentration uniform through the vessel and equal to the concentration in the outlet stream, so the whole vessel volume reacts at the outlet concentration, the lowest in the system. Constant density keeps the mean residence time a property of the vessel volume and the flow alone. Tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run. The residence time distribution of the real vessel is therefore unmeasured: dead volume would shorten the effective residence time, and bypassing would let part of the feed leave unreacted, and either would put the conversion of the actual vessel below 87.1%. The neutralisation is fast enough, on these values, that conversion is high but not complete: the unconverted fraction leaves with the product stream and is set by the same two quantities. The figure is the ideal-CSTR conversion for the stated rate constant and residence time, and it is the reference value a tracer test on the vessel would be read against.
